The presidential use of assistant-to-the-president-type czars has 
elicited at least three kinds of objections. First, it has been argued their use 
obscures lines of accountability. When a czar inserts him or herself into 
policy discussion, it may appear to diminish the responsibility of cabinet 
officers or other officials who are ordinarily held answerable for policy 
initiatives within their areas of authority. The czar’s involvement, 
especially because it may lack transparency, may mask the level at which 
critical decisions are being made, produce complaints from cabinet officials 
that their access to the president is being blocked, and confuse members of 
an administration as to the proper venue for pohcy discussion. Second, 
Members of Congress have objected that the power of czars implies that 
their appointment without Senate advice and consent is inappropriate and 
perhaps unconstitutional. (On the constitutional argument, see Mitchel A. 
Sollenberger & Mark J. Rozell, The Origins and Development of Executive 
Branch Czars, 25 J. POLICY HISTORY 638 (2013).) Congress’s last successful 
attempt, however, to impose advice and consent on close presidential 
advisers was in 1974, when the Director and Deputy Director of 0MB were 
so treated. A president’s need for close confidential advisers and the fact 
that they exercise no formal administrative powers have been sufficient, 
thus far, to rebuff additional calls for Senate involvement in their 
appointment—especially with regard to the National Security Advisor. 
Finally, some observers argue that “czars” are unlikely to accomplish much 
because they lack budgetary authority over the units they are supposed to 
help coordinate. Despite these arguments, presidents are still likely to find 
“czars” useful. John Podesta, who has served as a high-level White House 
official in two Administrations, has said: ‘When you have problems that 
really cut across a swath of agencies, it’s very important with respect to the 
president’s priorities to have a strong central place within the White House 
where people can get on the same strategy and that actions are keyed up 
and accountability exists.” Quoted in BARBARA L. SCHWEMLE, ET AL., CONG.
